questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Berlin because I wanted to brush up on my German while experiencing living in a larger European city with a vibrant cultural and musical scene. The academic aspect was only partially important in my case, but I was positively surprised in some areas and less so in others. Specifically, the academic level varied across available subjects, so you can both choose 'hard' and 'easy' courses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The only thing I would change is my choice of accommodation. I had not thought it important until I tried living far from the center, in a pleasant but remote area. Specifically I lived in Allee der Kosmonauten, which is a cheap and decent dorm and one of the options offered to Humboldt exchange students. It's unfortounately quite far from the center and from my faculty, the business faculty,, albeit with a tram connection, and grocery stores 15-20 min by foot away. That's not necessarily a problem; some might call it a whiny luxury problem, especially when the dorm is cheap, but I do regret not paying more to live closer to the center or just within walking distance of a U- or S-bahn. That's just a personal preference. My 'regret' probably also stems from my specific room in the dorm; the apartments are either 2- or 3-room apartments with a shared bath/kitchen. I got the smallest room in mine, while my two roommates got 1.5-size and 2x size rooms, compared to mine, both with a mini-balcony. Their rent was only marginally higher; 30-40 euro or so. Quite unlucky (and unfair, in my opinion).

That, and I would have participated in the month-long intensive language course in September. I unfortunately arrived in the second half of September so couldn't participate, but I wish I had arrived earlier - don't miss out on that for language skills and social connections!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a bit of a mixed bag. Information was relatively easy to get once you actually arrived, but the pre-arrival information was pretty lackluster - especially if you needed any 'seminar' courses for one reason or another, a good chunk of which already had their 'application deadlines' passed by the 1. of October. The semester officially starts on the 1. of October, but classes in reality only start two weeks later, and those are introduction classes - would have been nice to know. All of this applies to my own faculty, WiWi, to be clear. An introduction event was held a week before the start of classes; we were informed of said event by mail a day or two before it was to take place. During the event we found out that it was directed at both bachelor's and master's students (I am a master's). After the event the student council had organized a sightseeing-on-campus walking tour and a subsequent meet n greet - it was only here that I found out that the official event, and the subsequent social event, was not something specific to exchange students, of which there were few (which is not an issue!), but also for all people beginning their education at the faculty. It was fun and good from a social POV, but just a tad confusing and could have been better communicated beforehand. The seminar stuff mentioned earlier especially.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I turned up at the Erasmus/international coordinating office at the first day and got held with what I needed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Comments are mostly directed at pre-arrival, not so much upon arrival.

questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found accommodation through the assistance of the university, so 'pretty easy'.

That's just a personal preference. My 'regret' probably also stems from my specific room in the dorm; the apartments are either 2- or 3-room apartments with a shared bath/kitchen. I got the smallest room in mine, while my two roommates got 1.5-size and 2x size rooms, compared to mine, both with a mini-balcony. Their rent was only marginally higher; 30-40 euro or so. Quite unlucky (and unfair, in my opinion).

Berlin has Facebook groups, as seemingly we're some of the only people using that anymore, for Danish expats who often look or are more willing to rent to Danes. Looking through those groups in good time before arrival would have been a good choice and opportunity for finding something closer to the center or a S/U-Bahn - definitely recommend doing that.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I ended up regretting my choice of accommodation, but not every university offers cheap dorm housing (roughly 340~ euros a month for a room), so I think the housing was superb, even if it didn't fit my personal preferences. I do think it's a shame that everyone in at least my dorm paid more or less the same price, but the rooms assigned were wildly different within-apartment.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The paperwork wasn't so bad in general, but you need to get a mandatory insurance exemption (given that you have travel insurance) and it's a bit confusing and not very well explained how you're supposed to do that prior to semester start. If you wish to take 'seminars' those are also both pretty confusing to get into. Some require sending an email with a motivational text for why you wish to take it, others just make you register and then if there's too many sign-ups (the registration slots are quite small/limited 30-50 or so for most) they just do a lottery. For context, you usually don't sign up to classes, you just sign up to exams in January / show up to the ones you want to take, but for seminars it's the more traditional pre-semester registration process that Danes are used to, except you don't know if you'll get a slot, you're not guaranteed a slot and some have registration deadlines before the actual introduction events, so you only find out about those once those deadlines have already passed.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The university answered questions and helped in regards to the mandatory exemption stuff, but in regards to seminars and planning classes you were more or less left to your own bureaucratic abilities and ability to make an overview.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I didn't get into some of the seminars that I wanted, but got into others. You're very much left to your own abilities here, so if you need seminars, you need to put in the work yourself beforehand. If you just need normal classes with lectures, you can just wing it on arrival.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All of the bureaucratic stuff is quite messy compared to the streamlined way KU students are likely used to and more things are required to be done by hand and then scanned/sent, such as signed documents - you can't just digitally sign them - but it's not so bad. My best advice would be to arrive in September, one month before semester start, and take the intensive language course. You can get a head-start on the paperwork required by doing so, not to mention the other benefits.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses varied wildly. I found the selection of available courses quite limited at my faculty, WiWi, so I struggled a bit to find interesting classes at first, but managed to find some interesting ones in the end. The average 'academic level' of the courses seemed lower than at KU, but this was offset by some courses being really tough and undemanding, so you can find those if you're really looking for them. If you're an Economics student, you can also take courses offered at the general Berlin School of Economics, which covers all the Berlin universities.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The exercise classes, at least those that I partially experienced, are mostly a student assistant going through solutions rather than you working through the problems yourselves - at least that's what it seemed like most of the time. The seminars can be tough and intensive, depending on the seminar, and some have pre-chosen topics to select with weekly meetings with a supervisor. The Danish seminar system is mostly a self-study / self-writing exercise; this is only true for some seminars at WiWi, as some seminars have 'normal' weekly lectures, some seminars just have weekly 'office hours' and other seminars have a weekly meeting with your supervisor and constant deadlines; the last part mostly applies to the Information Systems seminar.

All of the normal/none-seminar exams at WiWi are done by hand, unfortounately, so be prepared for that. Moreover, the exams are very short, 60-120 minutes, so coming from Denmark it really becomes a question of time management like never before - at least if you write significantly slower by hand, like I do, and writing text answers on physical paper therefore becomes a huge travesty time-wise,.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: For the Fall I can especially recommend the Information Systems seminar, which is really demanding and though for those not used to coding in Python / machine learning, but also really rewarding. Helmut Lütkepohl's SVAR intensive course in October is also a big recommendation, but it takes place outside of Humboldt/WiWi's usual setup and you have to manually register by email (sidenote; the last week of October you write a short self-chosen exam paper; I was unfortunately sick during that period and didn't complete the course, but it's an excellent course nonetheless, as Helmut is literally the man who wrote the textbook used by KU on the topic)

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Of unexpected costs: a relatively small license fee required by the municipality; requires you actually registering with them, though.

General comments:

Humboldt required an up-front registration fee of roughly 200~ euro upon registration. The fee is not for tuition, but a sort of fee for the student council and includes a transportation card for the entirety of Berlin for the duration of the semester; a really good deal, all in all. Not sure if that'll still be the case in the future, but it was when I went in the autumn/winter semester of 2023/2024.

I did not buy a separate travel insurance but used the insurance included in my DJØF general insurance. The travel insurance there lasts for 120 days (or something like that), but those days 'reset' if you stay in Denmark for 24 hours throughout your stay; I had to visit home for various reasons a few times during my stay in Berlin, so could basically rely on said insurance for the entirety of the stay without any top-ups. Other fees therefore covers those costs along with a cheap gym membership.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food and grocery shopping was way more expensive than I had anticipated. Some grocery items were more expensive than they would be in Denmark. Anything sugar-related was way less expensive, while some things, eg. a fruit like kiwi, was significantly more expensive than what you could often find on offer in a Danish supermarket. Coffee is way cheaper. Going out (clubbing, drinking, etc) is cheaper, but not by much. Museum entry is somewhat cheaper, but varies across museums. The opera, at least the Staatopera, is WAY cheaper and easily recommended.

If you visited Berlin prior to corona and the start of the Ukraine-Russia War (of 2022), be aware that the price level is significantly higher now than it was previously - at least that was the case when I went, so don't expect to live the high life on a shoestring budget.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: My faculty's, WiWi, student council did do some social events and were cool folks, but it's not a big faculty so don't expect anything grandiose. The faculty building closes at 21.00 and the social events were mostly dozens of people going to a nearby bar after a student council meeting (which is held in German). Humboldt does offer a bunch of sports classes and a gym (I think?), which are mostly reasonably priced, but by the time you'll find out about them a lot of the interesting ones will be filled and some activities like tennis might be held very far in the outskirts of 'urban' Berlin, so the travel time alone is a huge disincentive. I just went with a cheap local 24/7 local gym instead. There was also some random Erasmus events/parties sometimes unrelated to Humboldt, but I never went and they didn't seem terribly popular among people I knew.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Going clubbing in Berlin, especially during the warmer months, is a very unique experience - there's a Berlin aesthetic that is a good idea to familiarize yourself with before going, and you should probably learn a few German phrases at a minimum, but that's not strictly necessary unless you're going to somewhere like Berghain.

While there's a great variety of museums, what I really recommend of purely cultural activities is visiting the Staatopera next to the main Humboldt campus. You get 50% off as a student; the cheapest seats are consequently priced at as low as 13 €, with the cheapest viewing seats at around 20 €. Compared to what you have to pay in Denmark, it's a really great deal for 3-hour live performances of classic opera. The Staatopera is often quite filled, but sometimes you can pull a fast one and move to unoccupied 'better seats' shortly after the start of the performance - being a poor student comes with /some/ privileges, sometimes!

PS: If in doubt how to dress for a night out, dress in black, unless you're going to Sisyphos, where you dress colorful, or KitKat, where you dress according to that day's theme. Getting into Berghain is quite doable; if you just want to go to cross it off your bucket list, try going alone at roughly 3-4 am Saturday, i.e. 03.00 Sunday, while wearing semi-casual black or not too colorful clothing - not white sneakers! - and a backpack. The latter is to show you're a regular, even if it's empty, but having a pair of changing clothes in the backpack is not a bad idea. Be sober at the entrance, or at least appear to be. Good luck!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Berlin has a vibrant night life and cultural life, but visitting Potsdam, especially during the Christmas market(s) period, and other scenic locations outside of Berlin is quite easy and doable using public transportation.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. The academic and bureaucratic culture took some getting used to, as described earlier, but it wasn't that bad. One thing to keep in mind - the 'Germans use fax'-thing is literally NOT a stereotype or a joke. A lot of things in Germany are less digitalized than you'd think and cash is still king in Berlin, with quite a few places only accepting cash, eg. (none-chain) eateries, bars, bakeries and coffee shops,

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Attend the intensive language course if you can; you'll meet lots of other Erasmus people that way. If you're going to WiWi, most of the people you'll meet there are also new to Berlin and likely took their bachelor's degree elsewhere, so hang around for the introduction event(s) and join the chat groups. While I might have had some reservations about my dorm, I also met lots of cool people there. There's every opportunity to be social and find friends, so that shouldn't be an issue; just show up to things!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The extent of the use of physical paper documentation, the exam-by-hand-on-physical-paper-thing and the amount of cash-only places. The university bureaucracy and associated systems are also quite messy compared to KU.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Berlin is really more of a European melting pot than a bastion of German culture, outside of the public bureaucracy, that is, truth be told, so if that's your thing definitely go, but if you want to be local with the local Germans then there's better destinations than Berlin. I was quite satisfied, however.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. If you need/are going to take seminars, badger the administration for information beforehand - the information you'll get prior to arrival likely won't be sufficient.
2. Attend the language course.
3. Consider what matters to you in terms of accommodation and the associated tradeoffs.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not really - you should definitely go.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All of it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The bureaucracy and physical distance to the faculty.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
